definition: A deep, melancholic longing for someone or something absent that one loves.
etymology: From Portuguese, derived from Latin solitas meaning 'solitude'; documented in Portuguese literature since the 13th century.
exampleSentence: Listening to fado music filled her with saudade for the Lisbon summers of her childhood.

definition: A homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or one that perhaps never was.
etymology: From Welsh, combining 'hir' (long) and an older root meaning 'grief' or 'longing'; in literary use since at least the 18th century.
exampleSentence: Walking the hills above Snowdonia, he felt a sudden hiraeth, though he had never lived there.

definition: The practice of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread.
etymology: From Japanese, combining 'tsunde-oku' (to pile up) and 'doku' (to read); first attested in 1879.
exampleSentence: His tsundoku had reached the point where the stack by his bed doubled as a nightstand.

definition: A worldview centered on the acceptance of transience and imperfection in beauty.
etymology: From Japanese, combining 'wabi' (rustic simplicity) and 'sabi' (the patina of age); rooted in 15th-century tea ceremony aesthetics.
exampleSentence: The cracked teacup, mended with gold, embodied a quiet wabi-sabi she had come to prefer over flawless porcelain.

definition: Studied carelessness; the art of making difficult things look effortless.
etymology: Coined by Italian courtier Baldassare Castiglione in 'Il Cortegiano' (1528).
exampleSentence: He tied his scarf with the sprezzatura of someone who had practiced the gesture for years.

definition: The soul, creativity, or love put into something; the essence of yourself left in your work.
etymology: From modern Greek, from Turkish 'merak' meaning 'labor of love'.
exampleSentence: You could taste the meraki in every dish she sent out of the kitchen.

definition: An aching longing for far-off places one has never been.
etymology: From German, combining 'fern' (far) and 'weh' (pain); coined in the 19th century as an inversion of Heimweh (homesickness).
exampleSentence: Every globe in the bookshop triggered another wave of fernweh.

definition: A feeling of cozy contentment from simple pleasures, usually shared with others.
etymology: From Danish, borrowed from Norwegian 'hugga' meaning 'to comfort'; in modern use since the early 19th century.
exampleSentence: Candles, wool socks, and a slow stew bubbling on the stove: the apartment was pure hygge.

definition: Warmly intimate and snug, often describing a place or a shared moment.
etymology: From Norwegian, related to the verb 'kose' meaning 'to enjoy' or 'cuddle'.
exampleSentence: The cabin was small and badly lit, but the company made it utterly koselig.

definition: The Finnish practice of drinking alone at home in your underwear with no intention of going out.
etymology: From Finnish, combining 'kalsari' (underpants) and 'kannit' (drunkenness); officially recognized by the Finnish Foreign Ministry in 2017.
exampleSentence: After a brutal week, he declared Friday a strict kalsarikannit evening.

definition: The overwhelming urge to squeeze or pinch something unbearably cute.
etymology: From Tagalog, used in everyday Filipino speech.
exampleSentence: The puppy's wrinkled face gave her such gigil that she had to look away.

definition: One's reason for being; the convergence of what you love, are good at, can be paid for, and the world needs.
etymology: From Japanese, combining 'iki' (life) and 'gai' (worth); in use since the Heian period.
exampleSentence: After leaving the law firm, he spent two years searching for his ikigai.

definition: Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune.
etymology: From German, combining 'Schaden' (harm) and 'Freude' (joy); entered English in the mid-19th century.
exampleSentence: She tried to hide her schadenfreude when her rival's souffle collapsed on live television.

definition: A weariness or sadness from the gap between the world as it is and as one wishes it to be.
etymology: Coined in German by Jean Paul Richter in 1827.
exampleSentence: The news cycle left him with a low-grade weltschmerz he could not quite shake.

definition: Excess weight gained from emotional overeating; literally, 'grief bacon'.
exampleSentence: After the breakup he wore a fresh layer of kummerspeck and a sheepish grin.

definition: The perfect retort that occurs to you only after the moment has passed.
etymology: From German, literally 'staircase wit', mirroring French 'esprit de l'escalier' coined by Diderot in 1773.
exampleSentence: Halfway home he was struck by the most exquisite treppenwitz; it would have devastated her.

definition: A wordless, meaningful look shared by two people who both wish to initiate something but neither will.
etymology: From Yaghan, an indigenous language of Tierra del Fuego; cited as one of the most succinct words in the world.
exampleSentence: Across the dinner table they shared a long mamihlapinatapai about who would mention the engagement.

definition: The restless anticipation that makes you keep checking outside to see if someone is coming.
etymology: From Inuktitut, used among Inuit speakers in the Arctic.
exampleSentence: He paced the porch with classic iktsuarpok as the headlights of every passing car raised his hopes.

definition: Sunlight filtering through the leaves of trees.
etymology: From Japanese, combining 'ko' (tree), 'moreru' (to leak through), and 'bi' (sun or light).
exampleSentence: She paused on the trail just to photograph the komorebi striping the path.

definition: A profound, mysterious sense of the beauty of the universe and the sad beauty of human suffering.
etymology: From Japanese, central to medieval Noh theater aesthetics; from Middle Chinese terms for 'dim' and 'deep'.
exampleSentence: Standing alone at the edge of the cliff, she felt the yugen of the open Pacific.

definition: A gentle sadness at the transience of things, and a tender appreciation of their passing.
etymology: From Japanese; coined by 18th-century scholar Motoori Norinaga to describe the emotional tone of 'The Tale of Genji'.
exampleSentence: Cherry blossoms in their last days always stirred a quiet mono no aware in him.

definition: A flexible, frugal, often improvised solution to a problem.
etymology: From Hindi; widely adopted in business and design literature since the 2000s.
exampleSentence: His jugaad fix for the broken washer involved a chopstick, two zip ties, and ten years of confidence.

definition: A humanist philosophy that one's humanity is bound up in the humanity of others.
etymology: From Nguni Bantu languages of southern Africa; popularized in English by Desmond Tutu in the 1990s.
exampleSentence: The village's response to the flood was a textbook expression of ubuntu.

definition: A leisurely coffee break, often with pastries, treated as a social institution.
exampleSentence: Meetings paused at three for an obligatory fika, and the office hummed back to life afterward.

definition: Not too much, not too little; just the right amount.
etymology: From Swedish; folk etymology ties it to 'laget om' (around the team), referring to Viking-era shared drinking horns.
exampleSentence: Her wardrobe was deliberately lagom: enough to be elegant, never enough to feel cluttered.

definition: A life lived in close communion with nature, as a guiding philosophy.
etymology: From Norwegian, popularized in 1859 by playwright Henrik Ibsen.
exampleSentence: Weekends meant friluftsliv: long hikes, cold lakes, and food cooked over a small fire.

definition: A clever, often improvisational workaround used to bend rules without breaking them.
etymology: From Brazilian Portuguese, diminutive of 'jeito' (way, manner); a recognized concept in Brazilian sociology since the mid-20th century.
exampleSentence: The clerk's jeitinho got our paperwork stamped two weeks early.

definition: The warmth of the sun in winter.
etymology: From Latin 'apricus' (sunny); coined in Henry Cockeram's English dictionary in 1623.
exampleSentence: The cat had chosen the one square of apricity on the kitchen floor.

definition: The earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry soil.
etymology: Coined in 1964 by Australian scientists Bear and Thomas, from Greek 'petra' (stone) and 'ichor' (the fluid of the gods).
exampleSentence: He opened the window to catch the petrichor before the storm arrived in full.

definition: The temporary inability to recall a word or name.
etymology: Coined by Carl Jung in the early 20th century, from Greek 'lethe' (forgetfulness) and 'logos' (word).
exampleSentence: He suffered a sudden bout of lethologica at the podium and called his old mentor 'that man'.

definition: Extreme difficulty getting out of bed in the morning.
etymology: From Greek 'dys-' (bad) and 'anistanai' (to rise); a clinical term used since the early 20th century.
exampleSentence: Mondays brought a dysania so heavy she negotiated with her duvet aloud.

definition: A soft, whispering or rustling sound.
etymology: From Latin 'susurrus' (a whisper); in literary English since the 19th century.
exampleSentence: A susurrus of wind through dry grass was the only sound on the hillside.

definition: The twilight; the half-light between day and night.
etymology: From Old English 'glomung', derived from 'glom' (twilight); revived by Scottish poetry in the 18th century.
exampleSentence: They walked back along the river in the gloaming, single file and silent.

definition: The wistful atmosphere of old bookshops.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows' (2012), from 'vellum' and 'petrichor'.
exampleSentence: She pushed open the door and was met with the unmistakable vellichor of a thousand secondhand novels.

definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
etymology: From Late Latin 'mellifluus', from 'mel' (honey) and 'fluere' (to flow); in English since the 15th century.
exampleSentence: The host's mellifluous voice could have sold sand to a desert.

definition: Denoting a period of time in the past that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
etymology: From Greek 'alkyon' (kingfisher), referring to a mythical bird said to calm the seas in winter.
exampleSentence: She often spoke of the halcyon summers spent at her grandmother's farmhouse.

definition: Strange and otherworldly in a sinister way.
etymology: From Scots, possibly from Middle English 'elfriche' (fairy realm); in literary use since the 16th century.
exampleSentence: An eldritch wind moved through the pines, though the air below was perfectly still.

definition: To mark or become marked with small patches of contrasting color or light.
etymology: From Middle English, of obscure origin, possibly Old Norse 'depill' (a spot).
exampleSentence: Late sun dappled the courtyard through the lemon tree.

definition: To express vehement protest or criticism.
etymology: From Latin 'fulminare' (to strike with lightning), from 'fulmen' (lightning bolt).
exampleSentence: He fulminated against the new parking rules for a full twenty minutes.

definition: To throw someone or something out of a window.
etymology: From Latin 'de-' (out of) and 'fenestra' (window); coined to describe the 1618 Defenestration of Prague.
exampleSentence: In a moment of frustration he nearly defenestrated his laptop.

definition: Going beyond what is required or expected.
etymology: From Late Latin 'supererogare' (to pay out beyond), via medieval theology.
exampleSentence: Her supererogatory kindness toward strangers became a quiet legend in the office.

definition: The realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows' in 2012.
exampleSentence: Stuck in traffic, he was hit with a wave of sonder for every other driver on the freeway.

definition: An intense, involuntary infatuation marked by intrusive thoughts of another person.
etymology: Coined by psychologist Dorothy Tennov in 1977 in her book 'Love and Limerence'.
exampleSentence: The limerence faded after six months, but the friendship that replaced it lasted years.

definition: The realization that the plot of your life no longer makes sense to you.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows', from Latin elements meaning 'a knot that lifts'.
exampleSentence: Halfway through his forties he experienced a quiet nodus tollens at the kitchen sink.

definition: The tendency to perceive familiar patterns, especially faces, in random stimuli.
etymology: From German 'Pareidolie', from Greek 'para-' (beside) and 'eidolon' (image); coined in 1866 by psychiatrist Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum.
exampleSentence: His pareidolia turned every car grille into a startled face.

definition: The tendency to perceive meaningful connections between unrelated things.
etymology: Coined by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958, from Greek 'apo-' (away from) and 'phaneros' (visible).
exampleSentence: Sleep-deprived and obsessed, the detective slipped into apophenia, finding clues in the wallpaper.

definition: A sudden thrill or shiver of emotion.
etymology: From French 'frisson' (shiver), from Latin 'frigere' (to be cold); in English since the 18th century.
exampleSentence: The opening chord sent a frisson down her spine.

definition: Relating to the state of partial consciousness just before fully waking.
etymology: Coined by Frederic W. H. Myers in 1903, from Greek 'hypnos' (sleep) and 'pompe' (sending away).
exampleSentence: In that hypnopompic minute, the dream still felt more real than the room.

definition: Relating to the drowsy state just before falling asleep.
etymology: From French 'hypnagogique', coined by Alfred Maury in 1848, from Greek 'hypnos' (sleep) and 'agogos' (leading).
exampleSentence: Her best ideas arrived in hypnagogic flashes she had learned to scribble down immediately.

definition: A neurological phenomenon in which stimulation of one sense involuntarily triggers another.
etymology: From Greek 'syn-' (together) and 'aesthesis' (sensation); coined in the late 19th century.
exampleSentence: Her synesthesia meant Tuesdays were always pale yellow, and Bach was indigo.

definition: A distortion of smell, often causing pleasant odors to seem foul.
etymology: From Greek 'para-' (beside) and 'osme' (smell); used in clinical literature since the 19th century.
exampleSentence: After her illness, a months-long parosmia made coffee smell like burning rubber.

definition: The inability to think rationally despite having adequate intelligence.
etymology: Coined by cognitive scientist Keith Stanovich in the 1990s.
exampleSentence: He was brilliant in his field and a textbook case of dysrationalia at the dinner table.

definition: A low, distant rumbling, like far-off thunder.
etymology: From Greek 'bronte' (thunder); used in 19th-century geological writing.
exampleSentence: A brontide rolled across the valley though the sky remained clear.

definition: A fine, misty drizzle.
etymology: From Middle English 'misellen'; in regional English use since the 15th century.
exampleSentence: By the time they reached the harbor, the rain had thinned to a soft mizzle.

definition: A warm, affectionate hug; also, a cozy little hideaway.
etymology: From Welsh, originally meaning 'cupboard' or 'safe place'.
exampleSentence: She gave the toddler a long cwtch before kindergarten drop-off.

definition: The amount that can be held in two cupped hands together.
etymology: From Middle English and Scots, from Old Norse 'gaupn'.
exampleSentence: He scooped a gowpen of well water and drank it straight.

definition: To hastily tidy a home in the brief window before guests arrive.
etymology: From a 19th-century New England English dialect word; revived in modern usage.
exampleSentence: She had ten minutes to scurryfunge the kitchen before her mother walked in.

definition: The sound of wind whispering through leaves.
etymology: From Greek 'psithuros' (whispering); used in 19th-century English poetry.
exampleSentence: He fell asleep to a slow psithurism from the elms outside the window.

definition: Strange yet marvelous; uncommonly wonderful.
exampleSentence: The valley after the snowfall looked positively selcouth.

definition: Admiration of a particular part of someone's body.
etymology: From Greek 'agastos' (admirable) and '-opia' (sight); a modern English coinage.
exampleSentence: He developed a quiet agastopia for the nape of her neck.

definition: A state of serene calmness, free from emotional disturbance.
etymology: From Greek 'ataraxia', meaning 'untroubledness'; central to Stoic and Epicurean philosophy.
exampleSentence: After the retreat she returned with a portable kind of ataraxia.

definition: A flourishing life of meaning and virtue, not merely pleasure.
etymology: From Greek 'eu-' (good) and 'daimon' (spirit); central to Aristotelian ethics.
exampleSentence: He measured the year not by his salary but by his sense of eudaimonia.

definition: An expression of doubt, real or feigned; a philosophical puzzlement.
etymology: From Greek 'aporia' (impasse), used by Socrates in Platonic dialogues.
exampleSentence: The seminar ended in a productive aporia, with everyone less sure than they began.

definition: The eerie atmosphere of a place usually bustling with people but now abandoned.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows', from Greek 'kenos' (empty) and '-opsia' (sight).
exampleSentence: The shuttered shopping mall was thick with kenopsia.

definition: The intense intimacy of looking into someone's eyes.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows', from Greek '-opia' (sight).
exampleSentence: Across the candlelit table they shared a long moment of opia.

definition: The subtle but persistent feeling of being out of place.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows', from Greek 'monachos' (alone).
exampleSentence: In the chic gallery he felt a steady monachopsis, like a seal beached on linoleum.

definition: Nostalgia for a time you never knew.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows'.
exampleSentence: Old jazz recordings filled him with anemoia for a Manhattan he had only seen in photographs.

definition: Sadness that you will never know how history turns out.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows', from 'ellipsis'.
exampleSentence: Reading about Mars colonies stirred a low ellipsism he could not quite name.

definition: An unfilled space or gap; a missing portion in a manuscript.
etymology: From Latin 'lacuna' (pool, gap); in English since the 17th century.
exampleSentence: There was a lacuna in the diary between June and September she could not explain.

definition: The taste of bliss in the absence of all thoughts.
etymology: From Sanskrit, used in Vedanta and Indian aesthetics.
exampleSentence: After meditation she lingered in a brief rasasvada before the day resumed.

definition: A state of musically induced ecstasy or emotional transformation.
etymology: From Arabic, central to classical Arabic musical tradition.
exampleSentence: By the third encore the audience had drifted into collective tarab.

definition: A heightened state of inspiration, passion, and authenticity in artistic performance.
etymology: From Spanish, popularized by Federico Garcia Lorca in his 1933 lecture 'Teoria y juego del duende'.
exampleSentence: The flamenco dancer had duende that night, and the room knew it.

definition: A place from which one's strength is drawn; a deep sense of being at home.
etymology: From Spanish 'querer' (to desire); used in bullfighting to describe the bull's chosen safe spot in the ring.
exampleSentence: The little bookshop on Calle Mayor had been her querencia for a decade.

definition: The leisurely conversation that lingers at the table after a meal.
exampleSentence: The sobremesa stretched until the candles had burned down to their holders.

definition: To take a walk in windy weather to clear one's head.
exampleSentence: After a brutal afternoon of editing, he went out to uitwaaien along the canal.

definition: To make something worse by trying to improve it.
etymology: From German, combining 'verschlimmern' (to worsen) and 'verbessern' (to improve).
exampleSentence: He verschlimmbesserned the gravy by adding a second cup of cream.

definition: A face badly in need of a slap.
exampleSentence: The smug commentator had a textbook backpfeifengesicht.

definition: The anxiety that time is running out to accomplish life's important things.
etymology: From German, literally 'gate-closing panic', dating to medieval city gates.
exampleSentence: Approaching forty, she felt a flicker of torschlusspanik whenever someone mentioned children.

definition: Vicarious embarrassment felt on behalf of someone else.
exampleSentence: Watching the toast go off the rails, she was overcome by fremdscham.

definition: A catchy tune that lodges itself in your head.
exampleSentence: He had a three-day ohrwurm from an ice cream truck.

definition: An intuitive flair or instinct, literally a 'fingertip feeling'.
etymology: From German, used in military strategy and adopted into business English.
exampleSentence: Her fingerspitzengefuhl for what a client really wanted made her invaluable.

definition: The reflective solitude felt when alone in a forest.
etymology: From German, combining 'Wald' (forest) and 'Einsamkeit' (solitude); a Romantic-era favorite.
exampleSentence: Two hours into the trail he reached a deep, unhurried waldeinsamkeit.

definition: An impractical dreamer with no business sense, literally 'air person'.
etymology: From Yiddish, with German roots; used in Eastern European Jewish literature.
exampleSentence: Her uncle was a charming luftmensch who reinvented his career every spring.

definition: To continue eating something delicious even after you are full.
etymology: From Georgian, literally 'I accidentally ate the whole thing'.
exampleSentence: He shemomedjamoed his way through the entire khachapuri.

definition: To hesitate when introducing someone because you've forgotten their name.
etymology: From Scots, in dialect use since the 18th century.
exampleSentence: He tartled awkwardly at the party, then improvised with 'you two know each other'.

definition: To gradually steal a neighbor's possessions by borrowing them and never returning.
etymology: From Rapa Nui, the language of Easter Island.
exampleSentence: Over the course of a year, his roommate had effectively tingoed his entire spice rack.

definition: The tender feeling once held for someone you no longer love.
etymology: From Russian, often cited in late 20th-century compendiums of untranslatable words.
exampleSentence: There was no anger left, only a soft razbliuto whenever she heard his name.

definition: A spiritual anguish, often a deep nostalgia or yearning with no clear cause.
etymology: From Russian; Vladimir Nabokov described it at length in his commentary on Eugene Onegin.
exampleSentence: On gray afternoons he was prone to a slow Russian toska.

definition: An ecstatic, joyful state of high spirits often expressed through celebration.
etymology: From Greek; central to Greek hospitality culture.
exampleSentence: By midnight the taverna was deep in kefi, with plates and feet flying.

definition: A deep sense of honor, generosity, and duty toward others.
exampleSentence: Helping the stranger fix the tire was a matter of philotimo, not heroism.

definition: Acting against one's better judgment.
etymology: From Greek 'akrasia' (lack of self-mastery); discussed by Aristotle in the Nicomachean Ethics.
exampleSentence: His New Year's resolutions died of pure akrasia by January 12th.

definition: Practical wisdom; the ability to discern the right action in a given situation.
etymology: From Greek 'phronesis'; a key virtue in Aristotelian ethics.
exampleSentence: Decades on the bench had given her a kind of judicial phronesis no textbook taught.

definition: Excessive, uncontrolled talkativeness.
etymology: From Greek 'logos' (word) and 'rhein' (to flow); used in medical literature since the 19th century.
exampleSentence: Three espressos in, his logorrhea was unstoppable.

definition: Having well-shaped buttocks.
etymology: From Greek 'kallipygos' (beautifully buttocked), name of an ancient Aphrodite statue.
exampleSentence: The marble figure was famously callipygian, drawing crowds for centuries.

definition: The rumbling sound made by gas moving through the intestines.
etymology: From Greek 'borborygmos', imitative of the sound.
exampleSentence: Her stomach delivered a thunderous borborygmus right in the middle of the silent meditation.

definition: An uncontrollable urge to dance, historically attributed to a spider's bite.
etymology: Italian, from the town of Taranto where outbreaks were recorded in the 15th-17th centuries.
exampleSentence: When the band hit the third song, she was struck with a happy tarantism.

definition: Fear of dinner parties or of conversing at meals.
exampleSentence: His deipnophobia meant he reliably canceled the morning of every reservation.

definition: A fight or struggle against an imaginary enemy.
exampleSentence: His online arguments were largely sciamachy with a phantom version of his uncle.

definition: The statistical study of elections and voting.
etymology: Coined in 1948 from Greek 'psephos' (pebble used in voting).
exampleSentence: Election week brought a small army of psephology bloggers to the airwaves.

definition: The insertion of a word into the middle of another word for emphasis.
etymology: From Greek 'tmesis' (a cutting); used in rhetoric since antiquity.
exampleSentence: 'Fan-bloody-tastic' is a textbook tmesis.

definition: A figure of speech in which one word governs two others in different senses.
etymology: From Greek 'zeugma' (a yoking); a classical rhetorical term.
exampleSentence: 'She broke his car and his heart' is a tidy zeugma.

definition: Ironic understatement in which an affirmative is expressed by negating its opposite.
exampleSentence: Calling the Pacific 'not a small body of water' is classic litotes.

definition: A moment of critical discovery or recognition, especially in drama.
etymology: From Greek; central to Aristotle's analysis of tragedy in the Poetics.
exampleSentence: The film's anagnorisis arrived quietly, in a kitchen, over cold tea.

definition: A sudden reversal of fortune in a narrative.
etymology: From Greek; another key term in Aristotle's Poetics.
exampleSentence: The novel's peripeteia hinged on an unsent letter.

definition: The release of strong emotions through art, leading to renewal.
etymology: From Greek 'katharsis' (cleansing); Aristotelian, central to tragedy.
exampleSentence: She left the theater wrung out, in the best, most catharsis-soaked way.

definition: Flirtatious talk that leads nowhere.
etymology: From Greek 'sphallo' (to cause to fall) and 'lalia' (talk); used in linguistic and rhetoric studies.
exampleSentence: The dinner party devolved into harmless sphallolalia by the second bottle.

definition: The act of loving in return; reciprocal love.
etymology: From Latin 'redamare' (to love back); an archaic English word revived in modern usage.
exampleSentence: Her letters told a long, patient story of redamancy.

definition: A hiding place; a secret repository.
etymology: From Latin 'abdere' (to hide); used in English since the 17th century.
exampleSentence: She kept her best chocolates in an abditory behind the cookbooks.

definition: To leave abruptly or stealthily.
etymology: American English coinage, 1830s, a mock-Latin formation.
exampleSentence: He absquatulated through the back door before the bill arrived.

definition: The philosophical doctrine that nothing can be known with certainty.
etymology: From Greek 'akatalepsia'; central to ancient Skeptic philosophy.
exampleSentence: By the end of his second whisky, he had embraced a cheerful acatalepsy.

definition: A feigned refusal of something one actually wants.
etymology: From Greek 'akkismos'; a classical rhetorical figure.
exampleSentence: His accismus about the corner office fooled nobody.

definition: Skilled writing in praise of trivial subjects.
exampleSentence: Her food blog was a masterclass in adoxography about sandwiches.

definition: A person who never laughs.
etymology: From Greek 'agelastos' (not laughing); used by Rabelais and later English writers.
exampleSentence: Her boss was the office agelast, and meetings ran accordingly.

definition: Difficulty identifying or describing one's own emotions.
etymology: Coined by psychiatrist Peter Sifneos in 1973, from Greek elements.
exampleSentence: Years of alexithymia made therapy feel like a foreign language class.

definition: The worst possible throw at dice; bad luck.
etymology: From Old French 'ambes as' (both aces); in English since the 14th century.
exampleSentence: The startup hit pure ambsace the month its server bill tripled.

definition: A phrase that can be interpreted in more than one way.
etymology: From Greek 'amphibolos' (ambiguous); used in rhetoric since antiquity.
exampleSentence: 'I saw the man with the telescope' is the schoolbook amphibology.

definition: Something out of its proper place.
exampleSentence: The neon sign on the medieval cathedral was a glaring anatopism.

definition: Full of windings and twists; tortuous.
exampleSentence: The coastal road was anfractuous enough to make passengers regret breakfast.

definition: Shaped like an eel.
exampleSentence: The dancer's anguilliform movement made the stage seem suddenly underwater.

definition: The cutting off of the final sound or syllable of a word.
etymology: From Greek 'apokope' (cutting off); used in linguistics since antiquity.
exampleSentence: 'Photo' from 'photograph' is a familiar apocope.

definition: To bask in the sun.
exampleSentence: The old dog apricated on the porch every afternoon, religiously.

definition: Shrewd, sharply perceptive.
exampleSentence: Her argute reading of the contract saved the company a fortune.

definition: Bad-tempered or melancholy.
etymology: From Latin 'atra bilis' (black bile), one of the four humors.
exampleSentence: He was unusually atrabilious all that winter.

definition: To dance clumsily but joyfully.
etymology: Of Middle English dialect origin; revived in modern usage.
exampleSentence: The toddlers baltered around the living room to the radio.

definition: A bottomless pit; figuratively, an insatiable appetite.
etymology: From Greek 'barathron'; in English since the 16th century.
exampleSentence: The teenager's metabolism was a barathrum no fridge could fill.

definition: A dealer in books, especially rare ones.
exampleSentence: The Paris bibliopole turned out to know more about her late father than she did.

definition: A person who talks at length without making sense.
etymology: From Scots 'blether' (nonsense) and 'skate' (term of contempt); popularized in America by the song 'Maggie Lauder'.
